The paper distinguishes sign language recognition (SLR) from translation (SLT) by defining their objectives and processes. SLR focuses on generating **gloss representations** (structured sequences of signs) from visual input, aiming to produce matching gloss sequences derived from sign language videos [S1]. In contrast, SLT involves creating **textual representations** that align with sign language videos, effectively translating visual signs into written or spoken text [S2]. 

Methodologically, SLR relies on techniques like **Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC)** for aligning keypoint sequences with glosses, while SLT extends this by incorporating **neural machine translation (NMT)** frameworks, such as an MLP followed by a translation network (e.g., mBART), to convert visual inputs into text [S6].
